rv.q: The Nance may turn out to be its dramatic high point.
The best thing about this play is that it’s positioned precisely at this intersection of comedy and pain.
Lane as the tortured soul at the play's heart is magnificent -- showing sides that are charming, witty, savage, self-destructive and yearning.
Lane is masterful, finding new depths in a well-worn sad clown persona.
It shows you the real pain of a real man, and makes you feel what he feels.
Lane, in the apotheosis of his sad clown routine, is sensational throughout.
With his hunger to entertain and his precision timing, Lane reminds us why he’s a vaudevillian master in those scenes.
This Janus-faced persona makes Mr. Lane a natural for the divided soul that is Chauncey, and he doesn’t disappoint.

So even when material lets him down, which it finally does in 'The Nance,' Douglas Carter Beane's splendidly ambitious but psychologically superficial tragicomedy, it's thrilling to watch Lane bond with a character who demands the full attention of so many gifted layers of him.
Douglas Carter Beane has written a play that's both hilarious and heartbreaking, examining the cost of hiding one's true self in a world that demands conformity.
What’s amazing about this scene is Lane is hilariously funny while he breaks our hearts.
Lane is funny, sad and touching as the conflicted Chauncey.
Lane reaffirms his status as one of the stage's brightest treasures.
It also allows Lane to combine his comedic persona with a tragic undertone, not unlike his fine performance in the 2009 revival of “Waiting for Godot.”
Lane's three-dimensional portrait of Chauncey Miles -- named after George Chauncey, whose 1994. Gay New York Beane consulted for background info -- is never a let-down.
I spent most of “The Nance” fascinated by the subject matter but frustrated by Beane’s execution.
Like Chauncy's two worlds, Beane's eventually crumble as well.
Beyond that, things get a little murky.

Thanks partly to a vivid performance by Nathan Lane in the title role, director Jack O'Brien's evocative production usually makes the most of Beane's troubling look at homosexual existence in Manhattan during the 1930s.

cn.t: Lane delivers a tour de force performance in Beane's ambitious but uneven play about a gay burlesque comic in 1930s New York. Critics praise the vivid period detail and Lane's tragicomic brilliance, though most find the drama doesn't fully coalesce.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
